section_entries.label: Introduction and main results
section_entries.mathematical_role: Defines the partition function, states Theorems 1–2 and tail corollaries, explains the critical freezing regime, and separates the proved upper bounds from the FHK conjecture.

unit_result_entry.title: Fractional moments reveal a critical square-root logarithmic renormalization
unit_result_entry.why_material: Theorem 1 uniformly bounds all fractional moments 0≤q≤1 by a scale containing a nontrivial denominator depending on (1−q)log log T. Optimizing Markov’s inequality in q turns this into a typical-size/tail bound smaller than the global mean by a square-root log-log factor.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: The short-interval second moment is a critical partition function
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: The paper treats the integral of |ζ|² over a fixed short interval as a statistical-mechanical partition function. Although its global t-average is of order log T, the motivating question is its typical size, exposing a distinction between an average dominated by rare events and a typical local mass.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: The exponent two marks the freezing transition and links partition mass to maxima
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Random-matrix ‘moments of moments’ motivate the distributional program, while the dominance scale of ζ moments explains why β=1 is the critical boundary between many and rare large values in a bounded interval. This identifies the partition function studied by Theorem 1 as the critical-chaos observable relevant to local maxima.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: At exponent two, rare Euler-product growth begins to dominate the short integral; multiscale barriers remove those rare trajectories and produce the square-root log-log normalization seen in low fractional moments.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The paper proves the upper bound for ζ and imports the corresponding random-model estimate; a matching ζ lower bound and full critical-chaos convergence are not established.
related_synthesis_entries.title: Critical chaos appears as a fractional-moment renormalization

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The q-dependent fractional-moment estimate is doing more than bounding moments: q is a tunable probe that converts a critical-chaos renormalization into a tail estimate. The optimized q detects a typical scale smaller than the ordinary mean.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Theorem 1 gives a uniform upper bound for fractional moments with 0<=q<=1 and a denominator involving 1+(1-q)sqrt(log log T). Markov's inequality, with q chosen from lambda, yields Corollary 1 and the upper typical scale log T/sqrt(log log T).
directed.conceptual_reading: A family of low moments separates bulk behavior from rare events more effectively than the first moment. The square-root log-log factor is the critical renormalization that the q-profile exposes.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Optimizing Markov's inequality over q bridges an analytic fractional-moment curve to a probability tail statement; the variable q acts as a scale-selecting parameter.
directed.boundary_or_failure: Only an upper bound is proved here. The claim that the shape is best possible is motivated by the later mechanism, not established by a matching zeta lower bound in this unit.
directed.uncertainty: The theorem-to-corollary mechanism and optimized-q role are clear, but the extracted placement of fractional powers, the minimum in the tail bound, and exact q formula should be checked against the PDF.

section_entries.label: Proof ideas
section_entries.mathematical_role: Develops the random Euler-product analogy, smooth/rough factorization, barrier-event derandomization, and additional ingredients for the maximum theorem.

unit_result_entry.title: Cauchy localization and a lower smooth-factor barrier convert maxima into a ballot problem
unit_result_entry.why_material: For Theorem 2, Cauchy’s formula replaces an unknown maximizing point by integrals around a 1/log T rectangle. A fourth-moment argument shows a large total product usually forces the smooth factor above a threshold; after derandomization this becomes a terminal lower barrier, and a Gaussian ballot estimate yields the characteristic 3/4 saving.

unit_dependency_entry.context_note: Retains the stated union-bound efficiency, fourth-moment loss V, strengthened good event, and two barrier savings. The argument’s current non-sharpness is traced to the rough-factor fourth moment.
unit_dependency_entry.representation_dependency: Contour size, smooth/rough thresholds, V powers, and log-log exponents are extraction-sensitive and must be PDF-verified.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: A smooth/rough factorization isolates Euler-product structure without discarding large primes
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: The proof approximates ζ by a Dirichlet polynomial, then in mean square by a product of a short P-smooth sum and a longer P-rough sum. Only the smooth factor is converted to an Euler product and compared with a Steinhaus model; the independent rough factor contributes its mean square. Multiscale good events and a recursive q argument import the critical-chaos saving.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Keeping the rough factor preserves scale, while multi-band factorization may reduce the main loss
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Unlike earlier approaches that shorten prime sums or shift off the critical line, this method retains the large-prime contribution and pays for it only through mean-square control. The author proposes—without checked details—splitting into more prime bands so successive largeness transfers incur smaller losses.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: Cauchy localization turns a point maximum into averaged contour mass; the fourth-moment lemma forces that mass through a large smooth factor, so after derandomization the problem is a Gaussian path staying below an upper barrier and ending in a narrow high window, yielding the 3/4 correction.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: This proves only an upper tail with iterated-log losses; the full FHK distribution and matching lower tail remain conjectural.
related_synthesis_entries.title: A local maximum becomes a two-barrier path event

related_synthesis_entries.claim: The non-sharp factor originates largely in exporting largeness across one coarse smooth/rough split by a fourth moment. Introducing several prime bands could transfer largeness incrementally and shrink this loss, but a sharp result would also require stronger probabilistic and rough-factor control.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The multi-band method is an unchecked proposal in the source, not an implemented theorem or validated improvement.
related_synthesis_entries.title: The principal loss has a concrete multi-scale repair proposal

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: A pointwise maximum is made averageable by Cauchy localization, then a fourth-moment sieve forces any surviving large value through the structured smooth factor. The added lower endpoint turns the familiar upper barrier into a ballot event and creates the 3/4 correction.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Cauchy's formula replaces the unknown maximizing value by contour integrals around a box of side about 1/log T. After smooth/rough factorization, a fourth-moment estimate removes cases where the smooth factor is at most log P/V. On the good event, the remaining smooth factor satisfies both upper partial-product barriers and a terminal lower bound; a random ballot estimate supplies two savings.
directed.conceptual_reading: Localization converts an existential point into distributed mass that can be averaged. Largeness transfer then routes that mass into the representation with usable multiscale structure, where the terminal constraint changes the probability geometry.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The chain is maximum -> Cauchy contour integral -> smooth/rough product -> lower smooth-factor barrier -> Gaussian path event. The integrand is squared, so the path-level exponent translates to the 3/4 denominator in the zeta threshold.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The fourth-moment transfer pays a rough-factor loss and is identified as a principal source of non-sharpness. The argument gives an upper tail, not a matching maximum lower bound or the full FHK law.
directed.uncertainty: The mechanism is well supported, but contour dimensions, V powers, and log-log exponents require PDF verification.

supported: The span uses Cauchy's formula to localize an unknown maximizer to integrals over a 1/log T rectangle and explains how interval enlargement and summation remove its unknown position.

A fourth-moment estimate discards cases with a small smooth factor; the surviving random restriction combines upper partial-product control with a terminal lower bound and yields the stated 3/4 denominator.
The source identifies the V loss in the fourth-moment transfer as a key reason the result is not sharp.
inference: Describing the terminal lower bound as changing the probability geometry is a reasonable abstraction.
